4321.prule: Phrase-level penultimate prominence: the penultimate syllable of the last word of an intonational phrase (declarative intonation; citation forms included) is 'stressed' and surfaces with a non-contrastive long vowel (final light syllable extrametrical, unbounded right-headed domain, stressed monomoraic syllable becomes bimoraic). Phrase-medial words, even a subject NP forming its own phonological phrase, show no penultimate length. No word-level stress rule is stated; the language is a two-tone (H/L) system with phrasal and intonational boundary tones.
4321.srule: No secondary or rhythmic stresses in the analysis: one stress per intonational phrase, on its penult (Mutaka 2014 secs. 2-4). Only footnote 6 adds, without data, that 'the root vowel is usually considered as bearing a stress' (it hosts all phonemic vowel contrasts) and that the stem may be parsed into two unbounded feet, i.e. stress on the first stem (root) vowel and on the penult, final vowel extrametrical; which of the two is primary is not said.

4321.tone: Two-tone (H/L) language with falling tones and lexical tonal classes (Mutaka 1994; Kenstowicz 2008). 4322.prule: Primary stress on the initial syllable of the phonological word in every word type Reid treats: monomorphemic nominals, free particles and postpositions (p. 90); reduplications and compounds (initial syllable of the first morpheme, pp. 91-92); class-prefixed nouns (the prefix, as the initial syllable of the phonological word, carries the primary stress; class proclitics stand outside the word, pp. 93-95); simple verbs (initial syllable = bound subject pronoun, pp. 95-96); complex verbs (initial syllable of the auxiliary, p. 97). Weight plays no role; final syllables of nominals never bear stress.
4322.srule: Monomorphemic nominals, free particles/postpositions and simple verbs: secondary stress on every second syllable after the initial primary (3rd, 5th...), never on the word-final syllable. Compounds: secondary stress on the initial syllable of each non-initial morpheme regardless of syllable count (contiguous stresses occur). Simple verbs with an object-pronoun suffix: secondary on the suffix-initial syllable. Complex verbs: secondary stress on the initial syllable of the complex verb stem (copied onto both halves of a reduplicated root) and on the initial syllable of a serialised auxiliary; tense/aspect enclitics never stressed.

4324.prule: Prominence-driven (unbounded) weight-sensitive system: word-level (primary) stress goes to the strongest syllable of the prosodic word on the scale Quant > QualPW > Coda (CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV; within a quantity class vowel height a > e,o > i and diphthong > monophthong; closed > open only at equal vowel strength); among ties the rightmost is stressed; a light ultima (CV, CVN) is never stressed; a heavy (CVV, CVVN) ultima is stressed when it is the strongest syllable.
4324.srule: Foot-level (secondary) stress (C&M 2005, verb data): the prosodic word (excluding extraprosodic object/modal clitics) is parsed left-to-right into bisyllabic feet, non-exhaustively: no degenerate feet and no PrWd-final foot unless one is needed to put word stress on the strongest syllable, so a light ultima and, in even-parity words, the penult normally stay unstressed. Each non-primary foot is headed by its stronger syllable on the foot-level Strength scale Quant > Coda > QualFT (CVVN > CVV > CVN > CV; a > e,o > i; æi > i); when the two syllables tie, headship follows Rhythm: iambic by default ('stress is assigned to the second syllable from the left edge and alternatingly thereafter, excluding the ultima', p. 51), trochaic only to avoid a clash with a following stressed syllable (*Clash > Iambic > Trochaic). 4326.tone: Two level tones, H and L; the tone-bearing unit is the mora, and post-vocalic glides and sonorant consonants also carry tone; each mora of a long vowel is toned independently; falling and rising contours on bimoraic (CVV, CVC) syllables and rising-falling on trimoraic ones are analysed as H/L sequences (falling-rising is ruled out by the phrase constraint); on CVC syllables closed by an obstruent the obstruent mora's tone is realised as a contour on the preceding short vowel; within a phonological phrase an expected H on the syntactic head is dropped whenever combining the words' lexical patterns would create two non-contiguous H tones (pp. 249-250, citing Hayward 2000). On stress the source says only that Thompson's (1976: 484) 'tentative comments about stress' find 'no convincing evidence' and that his examples are better analysed as gemination of the following consonant. Thompson 1976 p. 484 itself gives §2.2 'Stress may come on any syllable and can cause change of meaning' with the 'CVCV -> 'CVCCV gemination rule, and §2.3 'At least two significant tones occur; normal and high' (desso/déssó, du/dú). Pronunciation guide (p. 22): 'á, é, í, ó, ú say these vowels on a higher or stronger pitch than the other vowels in the word.' Four patterns contrast in shape on the same final syllable (high-level vs upglide vs high-falling), so this is not accent placement alone; the tone peak is nonetheless positionally restricted to the final or penultimate syllable, and the choice among patterns is partly conditioned by the final segment (obstruent-final and i/u+nasal-final words high-level; a/e/o+liquid-final words upglide; open-final descending words penult-high; liquid-closed descending words final-falling). tn.translation: The Ndambomo tone system rests on the opposition between two level (punctual) tones: the high tone (mwánɛ̀ 'child') and the low tone (ŋwànɛ̀ 'mouth'). The following minimal pairs illustrate this basic tonal opposition: nʧì 'fly (var.)' vs ǹʧí 'neck' ... The mid tone, which is also attested, could be the realisation of a high tone before pause ... We have treated these falling tones as particular realisations of high before pause ... On nouns we have recorded the tone schemes L, H, LH and HL.

4344.tone: Two simple tones, high and low; no phonemic mid tone (De Boeck 1952: 9). Bokula 1982: 119: 'la langue ndunga ne possède que deux tons simples: haut et bas'... 'seules les voyelles sont porteuses de tons'... 'Les tons sont généralement fixes'. tn.translation: The tonological system has only two 'simple' tones; the high tone and the low tone. There is no mid tone with tonological value. The tones are fixed: i.e. the syllables in words always have the same tone. ... The noun radical can carry all possible melodies, namely: high-high, high-low, low-low, low-high, for two-syllable radicals; etc. If a radical of tonological type high-high or low-high has a suffix of type V, the noun has the melody high-falling or low-falling

4346.prule: Accent position is lexically determined: syllables are underlyingly marked or unmarked, at most one marked syllable per morpheme, and the marking is contrastive (tsifungú 'j'ai fermé' vs rifúngu 'nous avons fermé'; tsilátsa vs rílatsa, pp. 274-275). Feet are built post-lexically over the prosodic group: final syllable extrametrical unless marked, unbounded left-headed feet, an H on the last syllable of each foot, all H but the first of the group deleted. In a word in isolation the H therefore surfaces on the marked syllable (or, with two marked syllables in the group, on the syllable before the second marked one, e.g. tsionó wana wararu). No weight conditioning is mentioned.

4347.heavy: Diphthongs 'count as long' and are always stressed in disyllabic words; a syllable with a geminate onset attracts stress (and its vowel is not lengthened). Closed syllables do not count: (C)VCVC disyllables 'almost all have penultimate stress' and stressed vowels lengthen 'regardless of whether they are open or closed'.
4347.dflt: penultimate (~80-90% of all-light words; 29/33 (C)VCVC disyllables; almost all 3-4 syllable words without geminates), with lexically stressed exceptions (the minimal pairs)
4347.prule: Lexical (phonemic) stress: contrastive between otherwise identical disyllables (seven minimal pairs in (27), six of shape (C)VCV and one VCVC, e.g. /aˈɸa/ 'dream' vs /ˈaɸa/ 'fathom', /haˈla/ 'pot' vs /ˈhala/ 'rain', /aˈmaŋ/ 'grass sp.' vs /ˈamaŋ/ 'his/her own voice'), realized mainly by vowel duration; no stress minimal pairs among 3-4 syllable words.
4347.srule: Weak secondary stress on the edge opposite the primary in trisyllables whose primary stress is initial or final ([ˌqulanˈdaː] 'snore', [ˈhaːmaˌjan] 'your beard', [ˌwalaˈgːa] 'door'), and on the initial syllable of 4-syllable words, all with penultimate primary ([ˌtonuˈgasi] 'worm', [ˌqamiˈa͡ua] 'green snake'); none shown on penultimate-stressed trisyllables; words of 5+ syllables not discussed.
4347.quote: Stress is realized in Nedebang primarily by means of duration. In words without geminate consonants, vowels of stressed syllables, regardless of whether they are open or closed, are longer. In words with a geminate consonant, stress is attracted to the syllable with the geminate onset. In these syllables, the vowel is not lengthened. Stress in Nedebang is phonemic. Minimal pairs found in my database demonstrating the contrast are presented in (27). 4347.sec_quote: A weak secondary stress is found with tri-syllabic words that have their primary stress either finally or initially. This includes lexical words with a geminate consonant in the final coda. A weak secondary stress is also found initially on 4-syllabic words, all of which appear to have penultimate stress in my data.
